issues.legal_issue: A shrine is a public temple under the governing definition only if it is a place of public religious worship and is dedicated to, intended for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it.
material_facts: The shrine was built by the head of an institution whose grants were made for his maintenance and for feeding and aiding religious mendicants and travellers.
The shrine was treated as an adjunct to that institution, and the evidence supported that access depended on the head's permission rather than a public right of entry.
Some income from the grants was spent on worship at the shrine, but the grant records did not establish that the grants were made for the shrine or for public worship there.
The evidence did not establish that members of the public worshipped at the shrine as of right; evidence of visitors or public attendance at festivals did not establish such a right.
issues.conclusion: The shrine was not a public temple within the statutory definition, and the order classifying it as a temple was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 requires both a place of public religious worship and its dedication to, benefit of, or use as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it. Evidence that people visit or worship at a shrine is not by itself proof of public use as of right, since visitors may be permitted to enter a private temple. The presumption discussed in Mundancheri Koman v. Achuthan Nair—that temples and their endowments are public charitable trusts in parts of the Madras Presidency where private temples were practically unknown—is rebuttable; the evidence here rebutted it.

rule.if: temple_status_appeal and grants_for_maintenance_and_charity and shrine_as_private_adjunct and access_depended_on_permission and public_dedication_or_benefit_not_established and public_use_as_of_right_not_established

predicates.temple_status_appeal: The proceeding concerns whether a shrine qualifies as a public temple under a statutory definition.
predicates.grants_for_maintenance_and_charity: The grants supporting the institution were made for the head's maintenance and for charitable aid to religious mendicants or travellers.
predicates.shrine_as_private_adjunct: The shrine was established as an adjunct to an institution rather than as a separately endowed public place of worship.
predicates.access_depended_on_permission: People seeking to enter the shrine for worship obtained permission from its head or manager.
predicates.public_dedication_or_benefit_not_establi: The evidence did not establish that the shrine was dedicated to or intended for the benefit of the Hindu community or a section of it.
predicates.public_use_as_of_right_not_established: The evidence did not establish that the Hindu community or a section of it used the shrine for worship as of right.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a shrine's public-temple status, grants for maintenance and charity, its role as a private adjunct, permission-based access, and the absence of established public dedication, benefit, or use as of right lead to the conclusion that it is not a public temple.

issues.legal_issue: Entries in an Inam Register have substantial evidentiary value but must be assessed in the context of the other information in the register and the evidence about the grant, rather than accepted at face value in isolation.
material_facts: The register entries referred to the shrine and its worship, but also recorded that grants had been made for charitable feeding and support of the institution.
The original grants predated the shrine's construction, and other recorded details indicated that the grants were for the institution or its head rather than for the shrine.
Some descriptions of grants as supporting a temple or being dedicated to God were inconsistent with the chronology and with other details recorded in the entries.
issues.conclusion: The register entries were of great evidentiary value, but the entries in particular columns could not be accepted at face value without considering the other matters recorded in the entries and the surrounding evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal recognizes the substantial evidentiary value of an Inam Register prepared after official inquiry, particularly where original grants are unavailable, while also recognizing that such a report does not displace authentic evidence. The Court applied the principle that the register must be read as a whole and in context, not by isolating an entry in a particular column. The relevant inam-settlement rule referred to in the judgment was rule 3(1), concerning continuation of inams granted for religious or charitable objects or services.

predicates.inam_register_evidence_assessment: The proceeding requires the court to assess entries in a register concerning an inam grant.
predicates.isolated_entry_conflicts_with_other_regi: An entry in one part of the register conflicts with other information recorded in the same register.
predicates.grant_context_undercuts_isolated_entry: The chronology or other evidence about the grant undermines the meaning suggested by an isolated register entry.

issues.definition: In an assessment of register evidence, when an isolated entry conflicts with other register details or is undermined by the grant context, the entry must be assessed in context rather than accepted at face value.
